claims.text: Single-crystal FeNiCrMn is initially a single-phase FCC alloy.
The initial alloy is fully annealed and has minimal pre-existing dislocation density.
Severe lattice distortion in FeNiCrMn creates solute-induced local stress concentrators.
Severe lattice distortion produces a high lattice-friction stress or Peierls barrier in the FCC alloy.
The onset of yielding is dominated by athermal dislocation nucleation rather than thermally activated dislocation glide.
Dislocations nucleate at pre-existing solute-induced local stress concentrators.
Candidate nucleation sites include solute clusters and specific crystallographic defects.
Dislocation nucleation begins when local stress exceeds a critical nucleation threshold without thermal assistance.
Athermal dislocation nucleation causes the anomalous strain-rate insensitivity of yield strength.
Yield strength will remain nearly constant over a wide range of strain rates from 77 K to 600 K.
Yield strength will have weaker temperature dependence than in traditional FCC metals.
No phase transformation will occur during the onset of yielding.
Pure Ni and Cu exhibit a strong positive relationship between yield strength and strain rate.
The strain-rate and temperature dependence of yield in traditional FCC metals is caused by thermally activated dislocation glide.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains single-phase FCC.
The mechanism may fail if an FCC-to-BCC transformation occurs or strain rates reach a shock-induced phase-change regime.
A statistically significant increase in BCC phase fraction coincident with yielding would falsify the proposed no-transformation mechanism.
A strong positive dependence of yield strength on strain rate would falsify the predicted athermal behavior.
